title: Explain the Two Pointers technique — opposite-end vs same-direction vs fast/slow variants.
shortTitle: Explain the Two Pointers Technique — Opposite-End vs Same-Direction vs Fast/Slow

s1_definition.profdef: The two pointers technique uses two index variables that walk through a data structure, usually a sorted array or a linked list, to solve a problem in linear time and constant extra space. The three common variants are opposite-end pointers that start at both ends and move toward each other, same-direction pointers where a slow pointer and a fast pointer both move forward at different rules, and fast/slow pointers where one pointer moves twice as fast as the other to detect cycles or find a midpoint.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh is checking a long printed ledger of transactions at the National Bank of India. Instead of scanning every pair of rows, he places one finger at the top and one finger at the bottom and moves them toward each other, or he keeps one finger on the last "good" row while another finger scans ahead looking for the next valid entry. Two fingers, one pass, no photocopying the whole ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two pointers turns an O(n squared) nested-loop scan into a single O(n) sweep using two moving indexes instead of one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The two pointers technique uses two index variables that walk through a data structure, usually a sorted array or a linked list, to solve a problem in linear time and constant extra space. The three common variants are opposite-end pointers that start at both ends and move toward each other, same-direction pointers where a slow pointer and a fast pointer both move forward at different rules, and fast/slow pointers where one pointer moves twice as fast as the other to detect cycles or find a midpoint.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh is checking a long printed ledger of transactions at the National Bank of India. Instead of scanning every pair of rows, he places one finger at the top and one finger at the bottom and moves them toward each other, or he keeps one finger on the last "good" row while another finger scans ahead looking for the next valid entry. Two fingers, one pass, no photocopying the whole ledger.

**One line to remember:** Two pointers turns an O(n squared) nested-loop scan into a single O(n) sweep using two moving indexes instead of one.

sections.s2_technical:
The opposite-end variant works on sorted data. You keep a `left` index at the start and a `right` index at the end, and based on a comparison you move one of them inward. For example, to find a pair of account balances summing to a target you compare the sum of the two ends: if the sum is too small you move `left` up to increase it, if too large you move `right` down. In code: `while (left < right) { int sum = a[left] + a[right]; if (sum == target) return ...; else if (sum < target) left++; else right--; }`. Each element is visited once, so it is O(n).

The same-direction variant uses a slow `write` pointer and a fast `read` pointer moving the same way. The fast pointer scans every element, and the slow pointer only advances when a condition is met, which is how in-place compaction works. For example, removing zero balances: `if (a[read] != 0) { a[write] = a[read]; write++; }`. The slow pointer marks the boundary of the processed region.

The fast/slow variant moves one pointer one step and the other two steps. In a linked list this finds the middle (`slow` lands at the midpoint when `fast` reaches the end) and detects cycles (if there is a loop, `fast` eventually laps `slow` and they meet). For example: `while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }`.

A senior-level nuance is knowing the precondition for each variant. Opposite-end almost always requires sorted input, same-direction requires that you only ever need to keep elements you have already seen, and fast/slow requires a sequence you can advance deterministically. Picking the wrong variant, such as opposite-end on unsorted data, silently produces wrong answers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a sorted list of settlement amounts for the day, and the reconciliation team must find two settlements that together equal a disputed amount. Scanning every pair is slow when there are millions of rows. This is exactly how opposite-end two pointers works — because the list is sorted, moving the low or high finger based on the current sum finds the pair in one pass.

Problem 2 — After a batch run, the ledger array has many cancelled entries marked as zero, and we must compact the real entries to the front without allocating a second array. This is exactly how same-direction two pointers works — a slow write pointer builds the clean list while a fast read pointer scans everything.

Problem 3 — The audit team receives a linked list of transaction nodes and must find the middle transaction for a quick sanity check without counting the length twice. This is exactly how fast/slow two pointers works — the fast pointer reaches the end just as the slow pointer reaches the middle.

The code below has one demo class that shows all three variants on banking data: a sorted-amount pair finder, an in-place ledger compactor, and a middle-node finder on a transaction linked list.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: sorted amounts [100, 250, 400, 650, 900] with target 650; ledger [500, 0, 300, 0, 0, 900]; transaction list T1 to T5.

Step 1: For the opposite-end search, `left` points at 100 and `right` at 900. The sum is 1000, larger than 650, so `right` moves down to 650. The data array does not change; only the indexes move.

Step 2: Now sum is 100 plus 650 which is 750, still too large, so `right` moves to 400. Sum becomes 100 plus 400 equals 500, too small, so `left` moves to 250. Sum is 250 plus 400 equals 650, a match, and we return the pair.

Step 3: For compaction, the `write` pointer starts at 0. The `read` pointer scans each entry. When it sees 500 (non-zero) it copies it to position 0 and `write` becomes 1. It skips the zero. It copies 300 to position 1 and `write` becomes 2. It skips two zeros, copies 900 to position 2, `write` becomes 3.

Step 4: The first three slots now hold 500, 300, 900, and `write` equals 3 tells us how many real entries survived. The tail of the array still holds stale values but we ignore them.

Step 5: For the middle finder, slow and fast both start at T1. Fast jumps to T3 while slow moves to T2. Fast jumps to T5 while slow moves to T3. Fast's next is null so we stop; slow at T3 is the middle.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Opposite-end pair for target 650: [250, 400]
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Compacted ledger kept 3 entries: [500, 300, 900]
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Fast/slow middle transaction: T3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: sorted=[100,250,400,650,900] target=650
    │
    ▼
  Opposite-End Pointers
    │ left=100 right=900  sum=1000 >650 → right--
    │ left=100 right=650  sum=750  >650 → right--
    │ left=100 right=400  sum=500  <650 → left++
    │ left=250 right=400  sum=650  == → MATCH
    ▼
  Result: [250, 400]

  Input: ledger=[500,0,300,0,0,900]
    │
    ▼
  Same-Direction (write/read)
    │ read=500 keep → write[0]=500
    │ read=0   skip
    │ read=300 keep → write[1]=300
    │ read=0,0 skip
    │ read=900 keep → write[2]=900
    ▼
  Result: [500,300,900], kept=3

  Input: T1→T2→T3→T4→T5
    │
    ▼
  Fast/Slow
    │ slow=T2 fast=T3
    │ slow=T3 fast=T5
    ▼
  Middle: T3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The two pointers technique uses two index variables that traverse a data structure together to reduce a quadratic brute-force solution to a single linear pass with constant extra space. There are three variants I reach for. The opposite-end variant starts one pointer at the beginning and one at the end of a sorted collection and moves them inward based on a comparison, which is ideal for problems like finding a pair that sums to a target. The same-direction variant uses a slow write pointer and a fast read pointer moving the same way, which is perfect for in-place work like removing or compacting elements. The fast and slow variant advances one pointer twice as fast as the other, which detects cycles and finds the midpoint of a linked list.

The most important thing I keep in mind is the precondition for each variant. Opposite-end almost always assumes the data is sorted, because the decision to move the left or right pointer only makes sense when the values are ordered. If I apply it to unsorted data it will quietly give wrong answers, so I either confirm the input is sorted or sort it first and account for that cost.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used all three in the reconciliation service. I used opposite-end pointers on the day's sorted settlement amounts to find two settlements matching a disputed figure, same-direction pointers to compact a ledger array by dropping cancelled zero entries in place without a second array, and fast and slow pointers to jump to the middle transaction of a linked list for a quick audit sample without counting the length twice.

The reason this matters in banking is scale and memory. When a reconciliation batch has millions of rows, turning a nested comparison into one sweep is the difference between a job finishing in seconds and timing out, and doing it in place avoids doubling memory on a server that is already under load. Explaining the three variants, their preconditions, and a real use for each shows the interviewer that I understand not just the trick but when each form is correct.

keyPoints: Two pointers from opposite ends: pair sum, container with most water
Two pointers same direction: remove duplicates, merge sorted arrays
Three pointers: 3Sum — sort + fix one + two-pointer scan
Fast/slow: linked list cycle, middle element
